directions: Plant container-grown rootstock liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft or bud a desired orange, grapefruit, or other citrus variety onto the young rootstock; Carrizo is grown as an understock, not for its own fruit. A citrange hybrid between sweet orange and trifoliate orange developed in California, it is among the most widely planted citrus rootstocks worldwide for its strong resistance to citrus tristeza virus, good cold hardiness compared to purely tropical rootstocks, and production of high-quality, well-anchored, moderately vigorous trees compatible with most scion varieties. Its combination of disease resistance and adaptability to a range of soil types has made it a standard commercial rootstock choice, though it is sensitive to high-pH, calcareous soils where iron chlorosis can become a problem. Graft a desired named citrus variety onto young rootstock, and provide winter protection in the coldest parts of its recommended range, since the trifoliate parentage improves but does not eliminate cold sensitivity of the resulting tree.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Colt is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit. Bred in England from a cross of sweet cherry and Chinese sour cherry, it produces a semi-vigorous tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a standard seedling cherry tree, offering meaningful size control along with good compatibility across most sweet and sour cherry varieties and better tolerance of wetter soils than many other cherry rootstocks. Its moderate size control without the brittleness and disease susceptibility issues of some fully dwarfing cherry rootstocks made it a long-standing standard choice before newer Gisela-series rootstocks became widely available. Graft a desired named cherry variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and provide well-drained soil despite its improved wet-soil tolerance relative to other cherry rootstocks.

planting.note: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Mazzard produces a full-sized, long-lived tree.

directions: Plant stratified seedlings or bare-root liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Mazzard produces a full-sized, long-lived tree. A wild sweet cherry seedling selection and the traditional standard rootstock for grafted sweet and sour cherry trees for well over a century, it produces a large, vigorous, deep-rooted, long-lived tree with excellent anchorage and broad compatibility across cherry varieties, without the size control offered by modern dwarfing rootstocks like the Gisela series. Its reliability, wide soil adaptability, and long productive lifespan have kept it in use even as smaller, more precocious rootstocks have become popular, particularly where a large, permanent shade-producing cherry tree is desired. Graft a desired named cherry variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and give the eventual tree ample permanent space, since it grows nearly as large as a wild, ungrafted cherry tree.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Gisela 6 is a semi-dwarfing, precocious understock, not grown for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired sweet or sour cherry variety onto the young rootstock; Gisela 6 is a semi-dwarfing, precocious understock, not grown for its own fruit. Developed at Justus Liebig University in Giessen, Germany, this member of the widely adopted Gisela rootstock series produces a semi-dwarf tree roughly 70-80 percent the size of a Mazzard seedling tree, combining meaningful size control with earlier, heavier fruit production and good tolerance of a range of soil types compared to more fully dwarfing rootstocks in the same series. Its combination of moderate size control, precocious early bearing, and good vigor and anchorage without requiring permanent staking has made it one of the most popular modern cherry rootstocks for both commercial and home orchards. Graft a desired named cherry variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect fruiting within two to three years, notably earlier than on a seedling Mazzard rootstock.

scientific_name: Vitis riparia x Vitis rupestris '3309 Couderc'

planting.note: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; 3309 Couderc is grown as a phylloxera-resistant understock, not for its own fruit.

directions: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; 3309 Couderc is grown as a phylloxera-resistant understock, not for its own fruit. A classic French-American hybrid rootstock bred in the nineteenth century from two native North American grape species specifically to resist the root-feeding phylloxera aphid that devastated European wine grape vineyards, it remains one of the most widely planted grape rootstocks worldwide for its reliable phylloxera and some nematode resistance, moderate vigor, and good performance in well-drained, moderately fertile soils. Its long track record and predictable, moderate vigor have made it a benchmark rootstock against which many newer selections are compared, though it is less well suited to very dry or high-lime soils than some other rootstock options. Graft a desired named wine or table grape variety onto young rootstock, and provide well-drained soil, since it performs poorly in wet or poorly aerated ground.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired plum or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; St. Julien A is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired plum or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; St. Julien A is a semi-vigorous understock, not grown for its own fruit. A selection of the wild bullace or damson-type plum long used as the traditional English standard rootstock for grafted plums, gages, and apricots, it produces a semi-vigorous tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a full seedling tree, with good compatibility across most plum and apricot varieties and reasonable tolerance of heavier soils compared to some other stone fruit rootstocks. Its long track record of reliable size control and broad graft compatibility has kept it in wide use for both commercial and home orchard plum and apricot production. Graft a desired named plum or apricot variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect earlier bearing and a more manageable tree size than on a vigorous seedling rootstock.

planting.note: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach, plum, or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; Krymsk 86 is a semi-dwarfing understock bred for wet-soil and disease tolerance.

directions: Plant bare-root rootstock liners in late winter while dormant in well-drained soil in full sun, then graft a desired peach, plum, or apricot variety onto the young rootstock; Krymsk 86 is a semi-dwarfing understock bred for wet-soil and disease tolerance. Bred at a research station in Krymsk, Russia, from a cross of cherry plum and peach, this modern semi-dwarfing rootstock produces a tree roughly two-thirds to three-quarters the size of a standard seedling peach tree, with notably better tolerance of heavy, wet, or poorly drained soils than most other peach and plum rootstocks, along with strong anchorage that generally does not require permanent staking. Its combination of size control, wet-soil tolerance, and good resistance to some soil-borne diseases has made it an increasingly popular choice for stone fruit orchards on less-than-ideal soils. Graft a desired named peach, plum, or apricot variety onto young rootstock in late winter, and expect strong, well-anchored growth even in soils too wet for many other stone fruit rootstocks.

planting.note: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; Dogridge is a highly vigorous, nematode-resistant understock bred for sandy Southern soils.

directions: Plant dormant rootstock cuttings or rooted liners in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun, then field bench-graft or bud a desired wine or table grape variety onto the young rootstock; Dogridge is a highly vigorous, nematode-resistant understock bred for sandy Southern soils. Selected from a wild Texas grape species adapted to the sandy, nematode-prone soils of the Gulf South and Southern Plains, it is among the most vigorous grape rootstocks available, imparting strong nematode and Pierce's disease tolerance along with drought resistance once established, making it a favored choice for vineyards planted on marginal, sandy, or previously grape-planted soils in the warm-summer South. Its exceptional vigor can be excessive on rich soils, where it tends to promote overly vegetative growth at the expense of fruit quality unless managed with appropriate canopy and irrigation control. Graft a desired named wine or table grape variety onto young rootstock, and reserve it for sandy, low-fertility, or nematode-prone sites where its vigor and resistance traits are most valuable rather than a liability.
